To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) vascular factors play an important etiologic role in the development of depression in the elderly, and (2) the association between vascular factors and depression is not restricted to poststroke depression but also includes depression with onset after age 60.

(1) the presence of subcortical vascular lesions is associated with a higher risk of developing depression; (2) depression is associated with the presence of sub-cortical vascular lesions; (3) depression is associated to a worse cognitive outcome; and (4) depression is associated, at least in part, to the presence of white matter lesions.
(1) vascular lesions in the subcortical structures of the brain are associated with late-onset depression and that (2) this association is not explained by the presence of vascular risk factors.

the association between vascular disease and late-onset major depression is real, but the nature of this association remains to be clarified.
the vascular lesions are neither necessary nor sufficient to induce depression.
depression is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, and cardiovascular disease is a risk factor of depression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pathophysiology of depression is complex and involves the interaction between multiple factors.
depression is a complex disorder that is influenced by genetic, biological, psychological, and environmental factors.
the vascular hypothesis is not a myth but a reality, at least for the late-onset depression.
